name: SciSpace
tagline: AI research assistant that searches a large academic corpus, chats with PDFs, and extracts structured data from papers.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The two halves of this product have very different difficulty. Chat-with-PDF, grounded citations, and a table that extracts "method / sample size / limitations" across a stack of papers is a well-trodden RAG build an agent can get working in a sitting. The literature search half is harder, but not closed: OpenAlex, Crossref, and Semantic Scholar hand you tens of millions of records and metadata for free, and Unpaywall finds the open-access PDF when there is one. What you cannot replicate is their parsed full-text layer and the extraction quality tuned on it, plus access to anything behind a publisher paywall. Call it a weekend that gets you 70 percent for your own reading list.
coreLoopDIY: Search open academic metadata APIs, pull the open-access PDFs, index them locally, then answer questions and fill a comparison table with per-claim citations back to the exact page.
requirements: An LLM API key for chat and embeddings
Polite-use contact email for OpenAlex, Crossref, and Unpaywall APIs
Local disk for PDFs and the vector index
Institutional access if you want anything paywalled, which the build will not fetch for you
whatYouLose: Full text of paywalled papers: your index is open-access only, which is a real hole in some fields
Their pre-parsed corpus, so your figure, table, and equation extraction will be visibly worse on messy PDFs
Polished mobile and browser-extension flows for grabbing a paper mid-browse
Reference-manager and Word/Overleaf style integrations for citation insertion
Whatever tuning they have done to reduce hallucinated citations, which is the failure mode that actually matters here
moatNotes: The corpus and its parsed full text are the asset. The chat wrapper around it is the commodity part, which is why every lab has a homegrown version.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a researcher's bottleneck is not "can I run a RAG pipeline", it is "is the paper I need in here and did you quote it correctly". Paying gets breadth including material your open-access-only index will silently miss, extraction that does not fall apart on two-column PDFs with nested tables, and a citation trail you can defend to a supervisor. The DIY build is genuinely good for a fixed reading list of 200 PDFs you already have. It is bad at the discovery step, which is the part people are actually buying.
notes: The reading half is a weekend; the finding half depends on whether your field publishes open access. Fields where it does, you barely need this.
prompt:
Build a local research assistant called "paperdesk". No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable: Python 3.12, FastAPI backend, SQLite with the sqlite-vec extension for embeddings, PyMuPDF for PDF text extraction, plain server-rendered Jinja2 templates plus htmx for the UI. No React, no Docker, no Postgres.

Secrets in .env: OPENAI_API_KEY, CONTACT_EMAIL (used as the polite-pool identifier for external APIs). Read them with python-dotenv and fail loudly at startup if missing.

Features, in scope:
1. Search: a query box that hits the OpenAlex works API and shows title, authors, year, venue, citation count, DOI, and whether an open-access PDF location exists. Paginate.
2. Add to library: clicking a result stores metadata in SQLite and, if OpenAlex or Unpaywall reports an OA PDF URL, downloads it to ./papers/. If there is no OA PDF, store the record and mark it "metadata only".
3. Manual upload: drag-drop a local PDF, extract title from metadata or first page, allow editing fields.
4. Index: chunk extracted text at roughly 1200 characters with 200 overlap, keep page number and paper id on every chunk, embed with text-embedding-3-small, store vectors in sqlite-vec. Make indexing idempotent and resumable.
5. Ask: a question box scoped either to one paper or to the whole library. Retrieve top 12 chunks, send to gpt-4o-mini with a system prompt that forbids any claim without a bracketed [paper_id p.N] marker. Render each marker as a link that opens the PDF at that page.
6. Extract table: user picks papers plus free-text column names like "sample size", "method", "main limitation". For each paper-column cell, run one scoped retrieval and one short LLM call, and store the source chunk. Show cells with a hover source and an explicit "not found" state rather than a guess. Export CSV.
7. Library view with filters by year and tag, and a delete that removes rows, vectors, and the file.

Out of scope, do not build: user auth, paywall bypass, any scraping of publisher sites, figure or table image parsing, citation-style formatting, reference-manager sync, mobile app.

Correctness rules: rate-limit external API calls to 5 per second and send CONTACT_EMAIL in the User-Agent. Cache API responses in SQLite. Never invent a DOI or a page number; if retrieval returns nothing above a similarity floor, answer "no supporting passage found in the library".

Deliver: requirements.txt, a single `python -m paperdesk` entrypoint that runs migrations and serves on localhost:8000, a seeded demo using three known open-access DOIs, and a README that states plainly that only open-access full text is available and what that means for coverage.
